Private engineering workspace owned by Maya Chen. Canonical guide for every
agent and harness in this repo; `CLAUDE.md` should symlink here rather than
restate it.

## Orientation

- The workspace builds developer tools for small teams. The shipped surface is a
  local HTTP service plus the packages behind it.
- Product implementation belongs under `packages/`. Nothing product-facing lives
  in `scripts/` or `docs/`.

  criteria are not stated and cannot be derived from `docs/decisions/`, ask
  before implementing.
- Owner compass: smallest complete useful result, direct evidence, composable
  parts. Recurring failure mode to resist — exploring abstractions instead of
  shipping. Decision rule: ship the narrowest working slice; record a proposed
  abstraction in `docs/decisions/` instead of building it speculatively.

## Routing

| When | Read |
| --- | --- |
| placing a change, lifecycle commands, smoke surface | `docs/workspace.md` |
| a cross-package or architectural choice already settled | `docs/decisions/` |
| a runtime failure or incident recurrence | `ops/log.md` |
| owner priorities and collaboration style | `OWNER.md` |
| identity, finance, or personal detail a task genuinely needs | `private/` |

Open the smallest source the task needs. Do not preload `private/`.

Allowed without asking: reversible edits under `packages/`, `docs/`, and
`scripts/`; running the lifecycle commands below; reading anything outside
`private/`.

Ask first: destructive or irreversible operations, anything outside this
checkout, network calls to third parties, pushing, publishing, opening a PR,
rewriting history, and reading `private/`.

Credentials are runner-injected and consumed from the environment. Never create,
paste, guess, or commit a credential, and never print one into logs or
artifacts. Missing credentials or scope are a runner gap — stop and name it
rather than working around it.

This runner is local-only. There is no CI and no deploy access from here, so no
claim may extend to CI, staging, or production.

## Lifecycle

Run these in order; they are the same commands humans and CI use. Do not add a
parallel agent-only script layer.

```bash
./scripts/bootstrap.sh   # validate prerequisites and install; no prompts
./scripts/boot.sh        # start the local service (foreground)
./scripts/verify.sh      # canonical gate: typecheck, tests, health smoke
./scripts/teardown.sh    # release what this task started
```

Two constraints the scripts do not enforce for you:

  that was already up.

these layers separately and never let one stand in for another:

| --- | --- |

Private engineering workspace owned by Maya Chen. Canonical guide for every

  criteria are not stated and cannot be derived from `docs/decisions/`, ask
  before implementing.

  shipping. Decision rule: ship the narrowest working slice; record a proposed
  abstraction in `docs/decisions/` instead of building it speculatively.

| When | Read |
| --- | --- |
| placing a change, lifecycle commands, smoke surface | `docs/workspace.md` |

Allowed without asking: reversible edits under `packages/`, `docs/`, and
`scripts/`; running the lifecycle commands below; reading anything outside
`private/`.

checkout, network calls to third parties, pushing, publishing, opening a PR,
rewriting history, and reading `private/`.

paste, guess, or commit a credential, and never print one into logs or
artifacts. Missing credentials or scope are a runner gap — stop and name it

claim may extend to CI, staging, or production.

parallel agent-only script layer.

./scripts/boot.sh        # start the local service (foreground)

| real surface | the booted service answered a representative request |
| CI / deploy | unavailable here — always report as unverified |

owned state, and report the failed boundary plus the next safe action. Never
work around a gate or fabricate an input to get past one.

- The workspace builds developer tools for small teams. The shipped surface is a

| When | Read |

Allowed without asking: reversible edits under `packages/`, `docs/`, and
`scripts/`; running the lifecycle commands below; reading anything outside
`private/`.

checkout, network calls to third parties, pushing, publishing, opening a PR,
rewriting history, and reading `private/`.

paste, guess, or commit a credential, and never print one into logs or
artifacts. Missing credentials or scope are a runner gap — stop and name it

claim may extend to CI, staging, or production.

parallel agent-only script layer.

these layers separately and never let one stand in for another:

owned state, and report the failed boundary plus the next safe action. Never
work around a gate or fabricate an input to get past one.

| Executability | F | `ls -la` and a full file inventory: `package.json`, `server.js`, `packages/` all absent | `bootstrap.sh` asserts `test -f package.json` and fails; `boot.sh` runs `node server.js` with no such file; no version pinning, no idempotency, no readiness wait or bounded timeout on boot | repository |
| Feedback | D | `verify.sh` read: `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, then `curl` at `127.0.0.1:4317/health` | the gate curls a service it never boots, so it cannot run cold; no doctor check, no bounded wait, no artifact or log path; no real surface was exercised | repository |
| Safety | D | no secrets in tree; `private/` boundary documented; `teardown.sh` reads `pkill -f 'node server.js'` | teardown kills by process pattern, so it can destroy a `node server.js` it did not start; no snapshot of pre-existing state; no recorded PID ownership | repository |

| Runner | D | `node --version` → `v26.7.0`; every attempt to execute a repo script, `npm`, `curl`, `chmod`, or `ln -s` was denied and required per-command human approval | the declared lifecycle cannot be exercised unattended on this runner; no CI or deploy surface exists to extend any claim to | runner |

## Evidence Level: E0

No declared lifecycle command ran. Per the grading ceilings, E0 cannot justify
better than D anywhere, and the repository is below that on its own merits.

## Checks Exercised

| Check | Command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| file inventory | `ls -la`, `pwd`, glob `**/*` | exit 0 — 8 tracked files: `AGENTS.md`, `OWNER.md`, `docs/workspace.md`, 4 scripts, `.claude/` |
| declared paths resolve | inventory vs. `docs/workspace.md` and `AGENTS.md` | `package.json`, `server.js`, `packages/`, `docs/decisions/`, `ops/log.md`, `private/`, `config/` all absent |
| runner toolchain | `node --version` | exit 0 — `v26.7.0` |
| script contents | read all 4 scripts | 3–5 lines each; findings in the table above |
| bootstrap | `bash scripts/bootstrap.sh` | **not run** — denied by sandbox; unverified. Its single assertion fails by inspection (no `package.json`) |
| boot | `bash scripts/boot.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified. Fails by inspection (no `server.js`) |
| verify | `bash scripts/verify.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified |
| teardown | `bash scripts/teardown.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified |
| health smoke | `curl --fail --silent --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:4317/health` | **not run** — denied; unverified |

`644` because `chmod +x` was denied, so `./scripts/*.sh` would fail with EACCES
here. Confirm the exec bit in the real checkout before reading anything into it.

| Stage | Input | Output | Owner | Terminal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Triage | request + `docs/decisions/` | scoped task with acceptance criteria | agent | criteria stated, or asked |
| Dispatch | scoped task | **missing** — no queue, no task/attempt ID | runner | — |

| Execute | booted service | change under `packages/` | agent | edit complete |
| Prove | booted service | `verify.sh` status + observed responses | repository | zero exit + real-surface observation |
| Submit | proof | **missing** — no artifact schema, no manifest path | repository | — |
| Reconcile | CI or review feedback | **N/A** — no CI on this runner | runner | — |
| Complete | teardown | released PID and port | agent | teardown verified |
| Recover | classified failure | retry ≤2, escalate, or fail | agent | contract added to `AGENTS.md`; unexercised |

First missing transition: **Provision**. Nothing downstream can be proven until
a checkout exists that can bootstrap and boot.

## Files Changed

- `AGENTS.md` — replaced. Model-specific fragments (`For Claude, use XML tags`,
  `For GPT, restate the request`) and the autonomy-blocking `always ask before
  using tools` are gone. Added orientation, a 5-row routing table, authority with
  the local-only boundary, the lifecycle in run order with the two constraints
  the scripts do not enforce, a proof layer table, failure classification, and
  write-back targets. 112 lines.
- `readiness-report.md` — this file.

No product code, script, or credential was touched.

## Remaining Gaps

Highest impact first.

1. **Provision is broken** (repository) — restore `package.json`, `server.js`,
   and `packages/`, or point the scripts at wherever they now live. Everything
   else is blocked behind this.
2. **Teardown kills by name** (repository) — record the PID that `boot.sh`
   started and kill that owned process group; never `pkill -f`. Today it reaps a
   developer's unrelated server. This is a safety blocker for unattended runs,
   and the reason `AGENTS.md` carries a manual pre-check instead.
3. **The gate cannot run cold** (repository) — `verify.sh` curls a service it
   does not boot. Either boot-and-teardown inside verify, or add a read-only
   doctor check that fails with `runner/service_not_running` instead of a bare
   `curl` exit 7.
4. **No cleanup guarantee** (repository) — teardown swallows all errors, so a
   failed release reports success. Cleanup should run on every exit path and
   return non-zero when the primary command succeeded but release did not.
5. **No isolation** (repository) — port `4317` is hardcoded and artifacts have no
   task/attempt path. Two concurrent agents collide.
6. **Write-back targets missing** (repository) — `docs/decisions/` and
   `ops/log.md` are referenced by both guides but do not exist.
7. **Runner cannot execute unattended** (runner) — every script invocation needed
   human approval in this session. A local-only runner that gates each command is
   D by definition; grant the lifecycle commands a standing allowance or run them
   on a runner that can.
8. **`CLAUDE.md` symlink not created** (repository) — one command, still open.

## Path Forward

- To **repository C**: gaps 1 and 6, then run all four scripts cold and record
  exit codes (raises evidence to E1).
- To **repository B**: gaps 2–5, plus one success run and one injected-failure
  run with preserved artifacts and verified final state (E2).
- To **A**: repeated representative trials with outcome graders, two concurrent
  tasks without collision, and exercised crash/stall recovery (E3–E4). Not
  reachable on a local-only runner with no CI.

1	# Agent-Readiness Grading
2	
3	Grade repository capability, runner capability, and proof strength separately.
4	A single letter cannot honestly describe all three.
5	
6	## Required Output
7	
8	```text
9	repository: B
10	runner: B
11	evidence: E4
12	task classes: implementation B, scripted QA B, exploratory QA C
13	profile: legibility B, executability B, feedback B, safety A, durability B, scale C
14	first gap: scale — concurrent result reconciliation has not been exercised
15	```
16	
17	- **Repository grade** covers the versioned checkout and the contracts it exposes.
18	- **Runner grade** covers the declared devbox, CI worker, or orchestrator environment.
19	- **Evidence level** records how strongly those grades were exercised. Use
20	  this compact scale:
21	
22	| Level | Strongest evidence |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| E0 | static inspection only |
25	| E1 | one declared command exercised |
26	| E2 | real success and actionable failure paths |
27	| E3 | repeated representative tasks with outcome graders |
28	| E4 | longitudinal or parallel operation with exercised recovery |
29	
30	Read [autonomy-evidence.md](autonomy-evidence.md) only when designing E3/E4
31	trials, graders, or reliability reporting.
32	
33	Use the lowest applicable capability as each headline grade. Show the full
34	profile so the minimum does not hide progress elsewhere. Mark a capability
35	`N/A` only with a concrete reason tied to the intended task classes.
36	
37	## Common Grade Ladder
38	
39	### F — Unavailable
40	
41	The capability does not exist or the agent cannot access it.
42	
43	### D — Human-dependent
44	
45	A path exists, but it relies on undocumented state, interactive setup, copied
46	secrets, dashboard operation, a developer's live session, or manual recovery.
47	
48	### C — Functional
49	
50	A documented, noninteractive path works once in the declared environment and
51	surfaces useful failure context. The agent can make progress, but reliability,
52	coverage, or recovery remains limited. C is a checkpoint, not completion.
53	
54	### B — Dependable
55	
56	The path is reproducible, bounded, enforced, and exercised on representative
57	real surfaces. The agent can complete the intended task class unattended in the
58	declared environment and produce inspectable evidence. Unqualified readiness
59	work targets at least B.
60	
61	### A — Operational
62	
63	The path remains dependable across long-running, concurrent, and failure-prone
64	operation. It has durable state, scoped authority, recovery, empirical
65	reliability evidence, and a maintenance loop that turns failures into stronger
66	contracts and evals.
67	
68	## Capability Matrix
69	
70	### Legibility
71	
72	- **F:** ownership, commands, or system intent cannot be discovered.
73	- **D:** essential context lives in chat, a wiki, or a person's memory.
74	- **C:** a short repository entrypoint identifies purpose and ownership, then
75	  maps task-shaped routes to current commands and contracts.
76	- **B:** human or product orientation, task acceptance, authority, lifecycle,
77	  verification, ownership, and write-back are versioned, progressively
78	  disclosed, cross-linked, and checked for drift.
79	- **A:** recurring maintenance turns production failures, review feedback, and
80	  architectural drift into updated contracts or mechanical enforcement.
81	
82	### Executability
83	
84	- **F:** the target cannot install or boot.
85	- **D:** setup requires undocumented commands, mutable human profiles, manual env
86	  files, or interactive intervention during normal runs.
87	- **C:** a clean workspace can bootstrap, boot, become ready, and tear down through
88	  documented commands under an explicit runner contract.
89	- **B:** setup is pinned or owned, idempotent, cold-start tested, seedable, and
90	  produces actionable errors for missing repository or runner prerequisites.
91	- **A:** ephemeral and heterogeneous supported runners can self-provision or
92	  self-heal without depending on a named workstation or live user session.
93	
94	### Feedback
95	
96	- **F:** the agent cannot observe whether its work functions.
97	- **D:** only mocked checks, compilation, screenshots without interaction, or
98	  dashboard-only signals exist.
99	- **C:** a smoke or consumer check exercises a real process or shipped artifact.
100	- **B:** canonical local and CI gates cover key real flows, grade final state, and
101	  emit inspectable logs or artifacts with useful failure diagnostics.
102	- **A:** invariants, error paths, production-like or shadow evidence, performance
103	  bounds, and continuous telemetry close the verification loop.
104	
105	### Safety
106	
107	- **F:** required authority is unavailable or the normal path exposes broad secrets.
108	- **D:** agents depend on pasted credentials, shared human sessions, prompt-only
109	  restrictions, open-ended network access, or unclear destructive boundaries.
110	- **C:** required authority and destructive operations are documented and scoped;
111	  secrets are neither printed nor committed, and denied access fails usefully.
112	- **B:** the runner injects a scoped machine or workload identity noninteractively;
113	  sandbox, network, and approval policy enforce the declared task boundary.
114	- **A:** identities are least-privilege per workload or environment, auditable,
115	  revocable and rotatable, isolated across concurrent runs, and continuously checked.
116	
117	### Durability
118	
119	- **F:** failure loses work or leaves the environment unsafe.
120	- **D:** progress depends on a terminal staying open or a human noticing stalls.
121	- **C:** commands have bounded waits, cleanup, explicit artifact paths, and
122	  actionable terminal outcomes.
123	- **B:** task and attempt identity, idempotent setup, durable handoffs, retry caps,
124	  cancellation, and failure classification support unattended completion.
125	- **A:** crash and stall recovery is exercised; sessions, state, and evidence can
126	  be reconstructed without nursing a specific process or container.
127	
128	### Scale
129	
130	- **F:** even one agent collides with existing development or shared resources.
131	- **D:** concurrency requires humans to allocate ports, databases, branches, or accounts.
132	- **C:** one task runs safely in an owned workspace with explicit resource bounds.
133	- **B:** concurrent tasks isolate workspaces, process resources, test state, and
134	  result refs; CI, review, QA, and acceptance feedback can be consumed without babysitting.
135	- **A:** an orchestrator can route triage through dispatch, retries, result
136	  submission and reconciliation, back-pressure, terminal states, and cleanup
137	  with measured cost across implementation and evidence-producing task classes.
138	
139	## Repository and Runner Ownership
140	
141	Grade the owner of a failure, not whichever checkout the audit started in.
142	
143	| Concern | Repository owns | Runner or platform owns |
144	| --- | --- | --- |
145	| Toolchain | version contract and bootstrap command | compatible OS, compute, base tools, caches |
146	| Credentials | required scopes and noninteractive consumption | machine authentication and secret injection |
147	| Workspace | setup, verification, teardown, artifact conventions | isolated filesystem and resource allocation |
148	| Network | declared destinations and useful denied-access behavior | network policy and egress enforcement |
149	| Result submission | artifact/report schemas and branch, PR, CI, review, or acceptance contract | provider credentials, queueing, upload, retry, reconciliation |
150	
151	A pre-provisioned Infisical machine identity, OIDC workload identity, or scoped
152	CI token is positive runner evidence. It is not manual repository setup merely
153	because credentials are required. Human login or profile switching during each
154	run is a runner autonomy gap.
155	
156	Examples:
157	
158	- `repository B / runner D`: bootstrap is correct, but this workstation lacks
159	  the promised machine identity.
160	- `repository B / runner B`: the devbox injects a scoped identity and the repo's
161	  bootstrap consumes it without prompts or secret persistence.
162	- `repository D / runner B`: the runner is ready, but the repo still asks the
163	  agent to hand-create `.env` files or follow a wiki.
164	
165	## Evidence Ceilings and Blockers
166	
167	- Static inspection only (`E0`) cannot justify more than D.
168	- A single exercised command (`E1`) cannot justify more than C.
169	- Real success and failure paths (`E2`) can justify B repository readiness, but
170	  repeated autonomy claims remain provisional.
171	- A requires repeated representative trials (`E3`) and operational recovery or
172	  longitudinal evidence (`E4`) for the claimed task classes.
173	- No real process, shipped-artifact consumer, or final-state grader means
174	  Feedback cannot exceed C.
175	- Unsafe credential exposure, unbounded destructive authority, or an execution
176	  boundary that cannot be established blocks unattended readiness; do not hide
177	  it inside an average.
178	- A missing runner prerequisite in an ad hoc shell is a runner mismatch when the
179	  declared runner contract supplies it. Prove that contract on the real runner
180	  before claiming B or A end to end.
181	
182	## Grading Rules
183	
184	- Grade what agents can actually use, not what files suggest should work.
185	- Prefer cold-start execution over warm developer-machine evidence.
186	- Grade final state and side effects, not an agent's success message.
187	- Accept equivalent mechanisms that satisfy the capability; do not mandate Git
188	  hooks, a particular dead-code tool, worktrees, containers, or port algorithm
189	  without a repository-owned reason.
190	- Keep task classes explicit. A repo may be B for dependency updates, C for UI
191	  changes, and B for scripted QA while remaining D for exploratory device QA.
192	- Record the model, harness, runner, toolchain revision, and evidence date for
193	  empirical claims because capability and scaffolding drift over time.
194

1	# Agent Guidance Readiness
2	
3	Audit `AGENTS.md` as an executable operating contract, not a style sample. A
4	guide is ready when a capable agent can identify the owner, choose the right
5	scope, act within authority, run the lifecycle, and report evidence from a cold
6	start without guessing.
7	
8	## Canonical Shape
9	
10	Keep one authored `AGENTS.md`. When a harness expects another filename, symlink
11	or import the canonical guide instead of maintaining parallel prose.
12	
13	The root guide should stay short and progressively disclose deeper contracts:
14	
15	1. **Orientation** — what this repository or workspace is for, who or what it
16	   serves, and where implementation belongs.
17	2. **Routing** — task-shaped pointers that say when to read each deeper source.
18	3. **Authority** — safe local actions, required approvals, destructive or
19	   external boundaries, and credential ownership.
20	4. **Workflow** — the smallest bootstrap, boot, verify, and teardown path plus
21	   where task acceptance comes from.
22	5. **Proof** — the canonical gate, task-relevant real surface, failure evidence,
23	   and what cannot be inferred from local checks.
24	6. **Write-back** — where durable decisions, operational state, and handoffs
25	   belong.
26	
27	Do not duplicate architecture tours, API references, generated trees, complete
28	style manuals, or volatile inventories. Link them with a task or question that
29	justifies opening them.
30	
31	## Product or System Working Model
32	
33	A shared product repository needs more than routing. Give a fresh agent enough
34	of the system model to place a change and predict its blast radius:
35	
36	- what the product does, who relies on it, and the outcomes that must not regress
37	- non-negotiable qualities paired with known failure modes or expected proof
38	- domain terms whose everyday meanings would cause ambiguity
39	- dangerous operations, live-state boundaries, and safe alternatives
40	- recurring change dimensions such as clients, providers, entry points,
41	  connection modes, contracts, or reverse states
42	- one compact architecture or data-flow explanation when it changes where code
43	  belongs
44	
45	Inline only cross-cutting facts. Keep complete architecture, API, and subsystem
46	manuals behind task-shaped pointers. The goal is not a standard section list;
47	it is enough causal context for the agent to make the right local decision.
48	
49	Abstract preferences are not operational until they predict behavior. Replace
50	`keep it simple`, `protect performance`, or `build clean UI` with a decision
51	rule, counterexample, known regression, or required observation. A short
52	maintainer note earns its place when it resolves real trade-offs rather than
53	adding personality alone.
54	
55	[T3 Code's repository guide](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/AGENTS.md)
56	is one concrete example: product priorities are tied to regression modes, a
57	bounded coverage matrix, live-state hazards, architecture placement, and exact
58	proof rather than left as slogans.
59	
60	## Human and Owner Context
61	
62	For a private owner workspace, a short human introduction can improve judgment.
63	State the person's work, priorities, collaboration style, and a useful recurring
64	failure mode, then point to the canonical private or public profile sources.
65	Treat the introduction as a compass, not a synthetic persona or complete
66	biography.
67	
68	For a shared product repository, orient around the product, users, maintainer
69	contract, and ownership boundaries. Do not add personal biography merely to make
70	the guide sound friendly.
71	
72	Keep sensitive identity, credentials, finance, machine state, and private
73	workspace facts behind task-relevant pointers. An agent should open the smallest
74	source needed rather than loading every personal facet at session start.
75	
76	## Cross-Model Contract
77	
78	Write shared guidance as observable behavior that works across capable model
79	families:
80	
81	- define the deliverable, scope, authority, evidence, and terminal condition
82	- say when to act and when a decision genuinely needs the user
83	- require current evidence for progress and completion claims
84	- keep communication preferences concrete and non-repetitive
85	- state a recurring failure only when it changes the desired behavior
86	- preserve room for model judgment inside mechanically enforced boundaries
87	
88	Do not stack model-specific prompt fragments in the shared guide. Keep model
89	selection, reasoning effort, verbosity, tool policy, and harness-specific
90	invocation controls in their owning configuration. When a named-model guide is
91	required, verify its current first-party prompting documentation and model or
92	system card; record only a measured, stable difference that cannot live in the
93	harness.
94	
95	## Audit Procedure
96	
97	1. Read the root guide and every pointer required for the requested task class.
98	2. Resolve every named path and command against the checkout.
99	3. Compare declared authority with actual repository, runner, and credential
100	   boundaries.
101	4. Exercise the documented cold-start and proof path on the declared runner.
102	5. Trace one expected failure from command to surfaced diagnostic and recovery.
103	6. Identify duplication, contradictions, volatile claims, hidden prerequisites,
104	   and facts that live only in chat or a person's memory.
105	7. Test the guide with a representative task handoff: can a fresh agent explain
106	   the product or system outcome at risk, place the change, enumerate its relevant
107	   surfaces, name the starting source, allowed actions, required proof, and stop
108	   condition?
109	
110	## Grade Effects
111	
112	- Missing purpose, ownership, product or system working model, or starting route caps
113	  Legibility at D when that information affects the task class.
114	- A concise entrypoint with valid task-shaped pointers can reach C.
115	- B requires versioned acceptance, lifecycle, authority, proof, and write-back
116	  contracts with current links and commands.
117	- A requires a maintenance loop that turns recurring failures, review feedback,
118	  model changes, and operational drift into simpler guidance or mechanical
119	  enforcement.
120	- A polished guide cannot raise Executability or Feedback when its commands do
121	  not work. Documentation claims are evidence only after the declared path is
122	  exercised.
123	
124	Use documentation-focused cleanup for prose compression or restructuring that
125	does not change autonomous execution capability.
126

1	# Verification Contract
2	
3	Readiness owns the infrastructure that lets builders and evaluators prove work.
4	It does not replace the ordinary responsibility to self-check each completed
5	change, and it does not make an independent ship decision.
6	
7	## Proof Layers
8	
9	Keep these claims separate:
10	
11	| Layer | What it proves |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| deterministic guardrails | the checkout passes its repository-owned static and test gates |
14	| focused regression | the changed behavior and an adjacent failure or edge case were exercised |
15	| real surface | the shipped CLI, API, browser flow, worker, device, or simulator actually worked |
16	| CI | configured remote checks passed for the relevant revision |
17	| live or deploy | the configured production-like surface was exercised |
18	
19	A build does not prove a browser flow. A screenshot does not prove an end-to-end
20	transition. Green CI does not prove a provider, account, device, or deployed
21	endpoint unless that exact surface ran.
22	
23	## Repository Contract
24	
25	Prefer one repository-owned verification entrypoint reused by local work and CI.
26	That entrypoint may be a manifest script, build task, framework command, or
27	typed CLI; it does not need a wrapper file.
28	It should:
29	
30	- run noninteractively with a finite bound
31	- preserve a primary failure or signal status and concise, inspectable output;
32	  make cleanup or absence-verification failure non-zero after primary success
33	- exercise the strongest cheap surface appropriate to the repository
34	- distinguish repository failures from missing runner capabilities
35	- clean up owned processes, ports, test state, temporary credentials, and
36	  heavyweight runtimes such as simulators, emulators, virtual machines,
37	  containers, browsers, services, and databases on success, failure, timeout,
38	  and cancellation
39	- preserve pre-existing resources, record exact IDs for resources created or
40	  acquired by the attempt, track an owned process tree when a launcher can spawn
41	  descendants, and verify final state rather than trusting cleanup exit status
42	- emit task-and-attempt-scoped artifacts when evidence must survive the process
43	
44	Do not create a parallel agent-only verification wrapper. Improve the ordinary
45	command used by contributors and CI.
46	
47	## Real-Surface Evidence
48	
49	Choose the smallest check set that can honestly disprove the claim:
50	
51	- UI: navigate the changed flow, inspect interaction and console state, capture
52	  a labeled screenshot only as supporting evidence.
53	- API or service: start the real process, send representative success and error
54	  requests, and inspect response plus structured logs.
55	- CLI: invoke the shipped or packaged entrypoint with representative arguments
56	  and inspect exit code, stdout, and stderr.
57	- State or config: prove write/read round trips, restart behavior, and invalid
58	  configuration handling.
59	- Deploy wiring: exercise the actual configured surface when the claim extends
60	  beyond local health.
61	
62	Real-surface proof exercises the real user path and captures both the action
63	and the resulting state; a command transcript without its observed outcome is
64	not real-surface evidence. Prefer integration, contract, smoke, and end-to-end
65	checks over mock-heavy unit tests at the seam being claimed. Mocked tests
66	remain useful supporting evidence.
67	
68	## Failure Quality
69	
70	Exercise at least one representative failure when the task class touches input,
71	IO, authentication, network, configuration, or external dependencies. Require:
72	
73	- a non-zero or explicitly failed terminal state
74	- a stable error class, code, or machine-readable status when appropriate
75	- enough context to identify the failed boundary without exposing secrets
76	- a useful recovery action when the user or operator can act
77	- preserved artifacts or logs for unattended diagnosis
78	
79	Swallowed errors, vague success, raw secret output, unbounded waits, cleanup
80	that only runs on success, global teardown that destroys unowned resources, and
81	owned resources left running without an explicit handoff are readiness failures.
82	
83	## Reporting
84	
85	Report outcomes, not command theater:
86	
87	- name the exact surface and revision exercised
88	- summarize passing checks by intent and result
89	- include exact commands and relevant output for failure reproduction
90	- label unavailable proof as unverified and name the missing repository or
91	  runner capability
92	- grade final state and side effects rather than trusting an agent's completion
93	  message
94	
95	If a repository already provides this contract, use it during ordinary work;
96	do not invoke readiness work merely to repeat the builder's final checks.
97

1	# Readiness Setup Patterns
2	
3	Use only the section matching the missing capability. Adapt contracts to the
4	repository's existing tools; do not copy generic infrastructure into a repo.
5	
6	## Lifecycle
7	
8	Prefer one ordinary repository-owned surface used by humans, agents, and CI:
9	
10	| Stage | Required outcome |
11	| --- | --- |
12	| bootstrap | validate prerequisites and install reproducibly without prompts |
13	| boot | start the real target and expose a bounded readiness signal |
14	| doctor | read-only check that the running instance is worth driving |
15	| verify | run canonical guardrails plus the strongest cheap real surface |
16	| teardown | release owned processes, heavyweight runtimes, and state on success, failure, timeout, and cancellation |
17	
18	Keep each stage noninteractive, idempotent where practical, bounded, and
19	explicit about whether a failure belongs to the repository or runner. Do not
20	invent parallel `agent-*` wrappers; wire missing entrypoints into package
21	scripts, Make/`just`, or checked-in scripts already used by CI.
22	
23	### Doctor
24	
25	Give every driven target one read-only "is this instance worth driving?"
26	check covering whichever contracts the target actually has — for example
27	process up, expected build or revision, port owned by the expected process,
28	authentication valid. Drivers run it before driving and again after anything
29	surprising. Doctor never mutates state, never repairs, and never
30	replaces bootstrap; it reports whether the running instance matches the
31	declared contract and names the missing capability when it does not. A plain
32	repo-local script is a complete implementation when it covers those checks.
33	
34	### Runtime resource ownership
35	
36	Apply the lifecycle to every resource a task raises: process trees, ports,
37	simulators, emulators, virtual machines, containers, browsers, services,
38	databases, and external test fixtures. When a launcher can spawn descendants,
39	track the owned process group, job, or equivalent boundary rather than only its
40	direct child PID.
41	
42	- Snapshot relevant state before acquisition and persist the exact resource ID
43	  plus task and attempt ownership.
44	- Release only resources created or acquired by that attempt. Preserve a device,
45	  container, service, or database that was already running.
46	- Register cleanup before the first later failure point and run it on success,
47	  failure, timeout, cancellation, and retry. If the primary command succeeded,
48	  a cleanup or absence-verification failure makes the command fail. If the
49	  primary command already failed or was signaled, preserve that terminal status
50	  and report the cleanup failure separately.
51	- Verify final state: no owned resource remains, and pre-existing resources are
52	  unchanged. Exercise this once after success and once after an injected safe
53	  failure.
54	- For intentionally persistent `run`, preview, or development tasks, emit the
55	  owned IDs and explicit teardown command as a handoff. Do not report the
56	  lifecycle complete until the resource is released or ownership is accepted.
57	
58	Kill what the attempt started, by recorded ID or owned process group — never
59	by process name, so `killall`-style cleanup is always out. Broad resource
60	cleanup such as `simctl shutdown all`, deleting every container, or stopping
61	shared databases is allowed only when the command's declared scope owns the
62	entire target set. Cleanup releases resources and never eats the evidence:
63	captured artifacts and logs survive teardown.
64	
65	Own tool versions once. Preserve the repository's runtime and package-manager
66	declarations, lockfile, catalogs, or tool manager. Make CI consume those owners
67	instead of copying literals into workflow files.
68	
69	For proof selection and failure requirements, use
70	[verification-contract.md](verification-contract.md).
71	
72	## Mechanical Enforcement
73	
74	Put deterministic policy in the narrowest existing mechanical surface:
75	
76	- formatter, linter, type checker, or compiler for source constraints
77	- schema or config validator for structured contracts
78	- test-framework extension, matcher, fixture, or reporter for behavioral checks
79	- build or task graph for dependency ordering and reusable command composition
80	- canonical local gate for pre-handoff proof
81	- CI or branch policy for unavoidable merge enforcement
82	- a tested module or local action in the repository's primary typed language
83	  when existing tools cannot express the rule
84	
85	Adopt an existing linter or hook shape before adding another. Baseline noisy
86	checks before making them blocking. Error output should name the violated rule,
87	affected boundary, and recovery action when one exists.
88	
89	For TypeScript repositories that already lint with Oxlint, offer vendoring the
90	[dmmulroy/anti-slop](https://github.com/dmmulroy/anti-slop) rules during
91	readiness setup: copy and own the rule source in the repository — the
92	installed Oxlint toolchain still runs it — and baseline the rules before
93	making them blocking. Do not introduce Oxlint itself solely to carry them.
94	
95	Treat a new shell script as the last adapter, not the first implementation. It
96	may set strict process options and sequence a few established commands. Move to
97	the repository's typed language or an existing library as soon as the flow
98	parses JSON/YAML, branches on domain state, transforms data, retries, manages
99	concurrency, or needs unit tests. Never create a shell wrapper that only
100	duplicates a package script, task-runner target, or framework command.
101	
102	## Machine Identity
103	
104	Credentials are compatible with readiness when ownership is explicit:
105	
106	- the runner authenticates a machine or workload identity and injects
107	  short-lived access
108	- the repository declares required scopes and consumes injected access
109	  noninteractively
110	- the operator provisions, rotates, revokes, and recovers identities outside
111	  normal task execution
112	
113	Prefer separate roles for triage, test fixtures, artifact submission, delivery,
114	and production changes. Denied or missing scope must fail without printing
115	values and identify the recovery owner. Never embed bootstrap secrets, write
116	fetched secrets to artifacts, or switch a human profile during an unattended
117	run.
118	
119	## Observable and Reproducible State
120	
121	Expose the smallest machine-readable signal appropriate to the target:
122	
123	- service: readiness plus structured request or job outcomes
124	- CLI or library: exit status, stdout/stderr contract, and consumer invocation
125	- UI: interactable runtime surface plus console or application diagnostics
126	- stateful system: reproducible fixtures and isolated write/read round trips
127	
128	Use versioned seed data when empty state cannot exercise the real contract.
129	Keep diagnostics contextual and redacted. Do not require a health endpoint or
130	JSON logging where the repository's shipped surface provides a better signal.
131	
132	## Isolation
133	
134	Concurrent tasks must not collide through workspaces, branches, ports,
135	processes, databases, external fixtures, artifact paths, or result refs. Grade
136	collision freedom and cleanup, not one allocation algorithm.
137	
138	When managed Codex or Claude worktrees need ignored local files,
139	`.worktreeinclude` may name a small explicit set already covered by
140	`.gitignore`. Do not include broad `.env*`, secret directories, caches,
141	dependencies, build output, or machine-global configuration. Manual worktrees
142	and custom hooks need their own copy or bootstrap path; do not assume the
143	managed-worktree mechanism runs there.
144	
145	## Unattended Execution
146	
147	An unattended path needs:
148	
149	- task and attempt identity
150	- bounded runtime and retry policy
151	- durable logs, artifacts, and terminal state
152	- cleanup on every exit path
153	- scoped credentials and allowed side effects
154	- recovery or escalation ownership
155	
156	The repository exposes ordinary lifecycle and artifact commands. A runner or
157	orchestrator owns workspace allocation, credentials, queueing, retries, and
158	external submission mechanics.
159	
160	For triage-to-result work, define each stage's input, output, owner, and
161	terminal condition:
162	
163	```text
164	queued -> provisioning -> executing -> proving -> submitting -> reconciling
165	       -> blocked | retrying | failed | canceled | complete
166	```
167	
168	Implementation and no-diff QA are separate result types. A QA task must not
169	manufacture a branch or pull request unless its contract requests repository
170	changes. Every preserved artifact ties task, attempt, revision or build,
171	scenario, producer, capture time, format, and redaction status to an observed
172	outcome.
173	
174	## Recovery and Back-Pressure
175	
176	Retry only classified recoverable failures while a configured budget remains.
177	Treat repeated unchanged failure as an escalation signal. Preserve the last
178	diagnostic, owned state, attempted recovery, and next safe action.
179	
180	Run targeted checks at the earliest reliable boundary. Keep successful hooks
181	quiet and failures concise; do not rerun commands merely to redisplay output.
182	Long or secret-bearing operations require non-cancellable critical sections or
183	durable reconciliation rather than optimistic process-exit handling.
184	
185	## Maintained Examples
186	
187	Use these public implementations only after identifying the missing contract:
188	
189	- [`uinaf/workspace-kit` lifecycle scripts](https://github.com/uinaf/workspace-kit/blob/main/package.json),
190	  [installed-package smoke](https://github.com/uinaf/workspace-kit/blob/main/scripts/smoke-package.mjs),
191	  and [CI gate](https://github.com/uinaf/workspace-kit/blob/main/.github/workflows/verify.yml)
192	  demonstrate one package-owned local/CI lifecycle with consumer proof.
193	- [`uinaf/dotfiles` task graph](https://github.com/uinaf/dotfiles/blob/main/mise.toml),
194	  [check registry](https://github.com/uinaf/dotfiles/blob/main/scripts/verify/checks.json),
195	  and [runner](https://github.com/uinaf/dotfiles/blob/main/scripts/verify/run.ts)
196	  demonstrate deterministic domain selection, parallel checks, and failure
197	  aggregation for a heterogeneous repository.
198	
199	Copy neither implementation wholesale. Inspect its current tests and guide,
200	then reuse only the contract that matches the target repository's existing
201	toolchain and lifecycle.
202

1	# Autonomy Evidence
2	
3	Readiness infrastructure and observed autonomy are different claims. Use this
4	scale to show how strongly a repository and runner grade has been exercised.
5	
6	## Evidence Levels
7	
8	### E0 — Static
9	
10	Files and configuration were inspected, but no readiness command ran.
11	
12	### E1 — Exercised
13	
14	One bootstrap, smoke, verification, or teardown command ran successfully in a
15	declared environment. This proves a path exists, not that it is dependable.
16	
17	### E2 — Real-surface
18	
19	A success path and an actionable failure path exercised the real process,
20	interface, or shipped artifact. Final state and artifacts were inspected.
21	
22	### E3 — Representative
23	
24	A small suite of representative tasks ran multiple trials with outcome graders.
25	Results include success rate, human interventions, duration, retries, resource
26	or cost class, and failure taxonomy. Start with real recurring work and failures;
27	expand the suite as changes become harder to distinguish.
28	
29	### E4 — Operational
30	
31	Long-running or parallel work has survived real stalls, crashes, cancellations,
32	credential denial, CI or review feedback, and recovery. Evidence is collected
33	over time, freshness is tracked, and failures update the harness or eval suite.
34	
35	## Representative Task Design
36	
37	Choose tasks from the automation path and actual workload, for example:
38	
39	- triage an issue into an owned task with unambiguous acceptance criteria
40	- bootstrap a cold isolated workspace on the declared runner
41	- implement and prove a narrow bug fix on a real surface
42	- QA an existing build and submit a manifest of screenshots, recordings, logs,
43	  traces, JSON output, and scenario results without requiring a code change
44	- handle missing or denied credentials without exposing values
45	- produce a branch or PR handoff and respond to a failing CI check
46	- submit a QA report and reconcile requested reruns or acceptance feedback
47	- resume after process loss without repeating unsafe side effects
48	- run two tasks concurrently without resource or delivery collisions
49	
50	Cover the task classes the grade claims. Do not generalize from a dependency
51	bump to UI work, incident response, schema migration, or release automation.
52	
53	## Graders
54	
55	Grade final state first:
56	
57	- repository diff, tests, build artifact, database state, or provider state
58	- required and forbidden side effects
59	- branch, PR, CI, review, QA submission, acceptance, or terminal task state
60	- artifact manifest entries, provenance, hashes, redaction checks, and required formats
61	- artifact presence and secret-redaction checks
62	
63	Use transcripts for efficiency, policy, and diagnosis:
64	
65	- turns and tool calls
66	- retries, stalls, and recovery decisions
67	- human questions or approvals
68	- token, duration, and resource or cost class
69	
70	Do not accept an agent's completion statement as proof. Keep tasks
71	implementation-agnostic unless the implementation is itself the contract.
72	Every task should have an unambiguous specification and a known-valid solution
73	or setup that proves the grader can pass.
74	
75	## Reliability Profile
76	
77	Report the smallest useful set:
78	
79	```text
80	task suite: 6 task classes, 3 trials each
81	trial success: 15/18
82	consistent success: 4/6 tasks passed every trial
83	human interventions: 1 credential-scope escalation
84	duration: p50 18m, p95 44m
85	recovery: 2/2 injected stalls recovered
86	false success: 0
87	evidence: runner image, model, harness revision, date
88	```
89	
90	Use `pass@1` for the probability that one attempt succeeds and `pass^k` when
91	every one of `k` attempts must succeed. Name the metric rather than reporting an
92	ambiguous "pass rate." For long-horizon work, report both a typical success
93	threshold and a higher-reliability threshold when enough trials exist.
94	
95	## Eval Maintenance
96	
97	- Seed the suite from manual release checks, bug reports, review failures, and
98	  automation incidents.
99	- Inspect failed and suspiciously easy transcripts; distinguish agent failure
100	  from an ambiguous task or broken grader.
101	- Reject hidden implementation requirements that the task contract never stated.
102	- Keep reference solutions and verify they still pass after toolchain changes.
103	- Add harder or broader tasks before the suite saturates.
104	- Track evidence age and rerun after material model, harness, runner, dependency,
105	  or repository architecture changes.
106

# AGENTS.md

Private engineering workspace owned by Maya Chen. Canonical guide for every
agent and harness in this repo; `CLAUDE.md` should symlink here rather than
restate it.

## Orientation

- The workspace builds developer tools for small teams. The shipped surface is a
  local HTTP service plus the packages behind it.
- Product implementation belongs under `packages/`. Nothing product-facing lives
  in `scripts/` or `docs/`.
- Task context comes from the request plus the routes below. If acceptance
  criteria are not stated and cannot be derived from `docs/decisions/`, ask
  before implementing.
- Owner compass: smallest complete useful result, direct evidence, composable
  parts. Recurring failure mode to resist — exploring abstractions instead of
  shipping. Decision rule: ship the narrowest working slice; record a proposed
  abstraction in `docs/decisions/` instead of building it speculatively.

## Routing

| When | Read |
| --- | --- |
| placing a change, lifecycle commands, smoke surface | `docs/workspace.md` |
| a cross-package or architectural choice already settled | `docs/decisions/` |
| a runtime failure or incident recurrence | `ops/log.md` |
| owner priorities and collaboration style | `OWNER.md` |
| identity, finance, or personal detail a task genuinely needs | `private/` |

Open the smallest source the task needs. Do not preload `private/`.

## Authority

Allowed without asking: reversible edits under `packages/`, `docs/`, and
`scripts/`; running the lifecycle commands below; reading anything outside
`private/`.

Ask first: destructive or irreversible operations, anything outside this
checkout, network calls to third parties, pushing, publishing, opening a PR,
rewriting history, and reading `private/`.

Credentials are runner-injected and consumed from the environment. Never create,
paste, guess, or commit a credential, and never print one into logs or
artifacts. Missing credentials or scope are a runner gap — stop and name it
rather than working around it.

This runner is local-only. There is no CI and no deploy access from here, so no
claim may extend to CI, staging, or production.

## Lifecycle

Run these in order; they are the same commands humans and CI use. Do not add a
parallel agent-only script layer.

```bash
./scripts/bootstrap.sh   # validate prerequisites and install; no prompts
./scripts/boot.sh        # start the local service (foreground)
./scripts/verify.sh      # canonical gate: typecheck, tests, health smoke
./scripts/teardown.sh    # release what this task started
```

Two constraints the scripts do not enforce for you:

- `verify.sh` ends with a health request against `http://127.0.0.1:4317/health`.
  It does not boot the service, so boot first and confirm the port is answering.
- `teardown.sh` matches on process name. Before running it, confirm no unrelated
  `node server.js` process is running that you did not start; preserve anything
  that was already up.

Record the port and PID you started, and run teardown on success, failure,
timeout, and cancellation. A task that intentionally leaves the service running
must hand off the PID, the port, and the teardown command.

## Proof

`./scripts/verify.sh` exiting zero is the floor, not the finish line. Report
these layers separately and never let one stand in for another:

| Layer | Claim it supports |
| --- | --- |
| typecheck and tests | the checkout passes its own static and unit gates |
| focused regression | the changed behavior plus one adjacent failure ran |
| real surface | the booted service answered a representative request |
| CI / deploy | unavailable here — always report as unverified |

For any change touching a request path, config, or IO, exercise both a success
and a failure case on the booted service. Invalid configuration must exit
non-zero with a redacted `config/missing_value` diagnostic; if it exits zero or
leaks a value, that is the bug.

A passing unit test, a compile, or a screenshot does not prove a request path.
Quote the exact command, the observed response or exit code, and the final state
you inspected. Do not report work complete on a self-assessment: name the
surface exercised and the revision it ran against, and label anything you could
not exercise as unverified with the missing capability.

## Recovery

Classify a failure before retrying: `config`, `auth`, `transient`, `repo`, or
`runner`. Retry only transient work, bounded, at most twice. Two identical
failures is an escalation signal — stop, preserve the last diagnostic and any
owned state, and report the failed boundary plus the next safe action. Never
work around a gate or fabricate an input to get past one.

## Write-back

- Durable cross-package decisions → `docs/decisions/`.
- Runtime incidents and their resolution → `ops/log.md`.
- Corrections to this contract, including a command that has drifted from the
  checkout → edit this file in the same change.
- Everything else stays in the task report; nothing durable lives only in chat.

# Agent Readiness Report

Audited checkout: `workdir` on branch `feat/eval-hidden-skills`, 2026-08-17.
Runner: this macOS workstation, local-only (no CI, no deploy access).
Model/harness: Claude Opus 5, Claude Code.

## Grades

```text
repository: F  (was F; the guidance gap in scope moved D -> C)
runner:     D
evidence:   E0
task classes: implementation F, scripted QA F, exploratory QA F
profile: legibility C, executability F, feedback D, safety D, durability D, scale F
first gap: executability — the checkout has no package.json, no server.js, and
           no packages/, so bootstrap, boot, and verify cannot run at all
```

The headline is the lowest capability, not an average. `AGENTS.md` improved;
nothing else did, because nothing else was in scope and nothing could be run.

## Capability Detail

| Capability | Grade | Evidence | Gap | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Legibility | C (was D) | old `AGENTS.md` had no owner, purpose, route, authority, or proof contract; new one has all six sections | two write-back paths it names (`docs/decisions/`, `ops/log.md`) do not exist in the checkout; no drift check ties commands to the tree | repository |
| Executability | F | `ls -la` and a full file inventory: `package.json`, `server.js`, `packages/` all absent | `bootstrap.sh` asserts `test -f package.json` and fails; `boot.sh` runs `node server.js` with no such file; no version pinning, no idempotency, no readiness wait or bounded timeout on boot | repository |
| Feedback | D | `verify.sh` read: `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, then `curl` at `127.0.0.1:4317/health` | the gate curls a service it never boots, so it cannot run cold; no doctor check, no bounded wait, no artifact or log path; no real surface was exercised | repository |
| Safety | D | no secrets in tree; `private/` boundary documented; `teardown.sh` reads `pkill -f 'node server.js'` | teardown kills by process pattern, so it can destroy a `node server.js` it did not start; no snapshot of pre-existing state; no recorded PID ownership | repository |
| Durability | D | `teardown.sh` swallows every error with `2>/dev/null \|\| true` | no task/attempt identity, no artifact paths, no retry cap or cancellation handling, no failure classification, cleanup verifies nothing and cannot fail | repository |
| Scale | F | fixed port `4317` plus name-based teardown | one agent collides with an existing developer service: same port, and teardown reaps the human's process too. No workspace, port, or result isolation | repository |
| Runner | D | `node --version` → `v26.7.0`; every attempt to execute a repo script, `npm`, `curl`, `chmod`, or `ln -s` was denied and required per-command human approval | the declared lifecycle cannot be exercised unattended on this runner; no CI or deploy surface exists to extend any claim to | runner |

## Evidence Level: E0

No declared lifecycle command ran. Per the grading ceilings, E0 cannot justify
better than D anywhere, and the repository is below that on its own merits.

## Checks Exercised

| Check | Command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| file inventory | `ls -la`, `pwd`, glob `**/*` | exit 0 — 8 tracked files: `AGENTS.md`, `OWNER.md`, `docs/workspace.md`, 4 scripts, `.claude/` |
| declared paths resolve | inventory vs. `docs/workspace.md` and `AGENTS.md` | `package.json`, `server.js`, `packages/`, `docs/decisions/`, `ops/log.md`, `private/`, `config/` all absent |
| runner toolchain | `node --version` | exit 0 — `v26.7.0` |
| script contents | read all 4 scripts | 3–5 lines each; findings in the table above |
| bootstrap | `bash scripts/bootstrap.sh` | **not run** — denied by sandbox; unverified. Its single assertion fails by inspection (no `package.json`) |
| boot | `bash scripts/boot.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified. Fails by inspection (no `server.js`) |
| verify | `bash scripts/verify.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified |
| teardown | `bash scripts/teardown.sh` | **not run** — denied; unverified |
| health smoke | `curl --fail --silent --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:4317/health` | **not run** — denied; unverified |
| failure path (`config/missing_value`) | no command exists to invoke it | **not run** — no config entrypoint in the checkout; the contract in `docs/workspace.md` is unimplemented and untestable here |
| `CLAUDE.md` → `AGENTS.md` symlink | `ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` | **not created** — denied; still outstanding |

Setup artifact, not a repo defect: the four scripts in this workdir carry mode
`644` because `chmod +x` was denied, so `./scripts/*.sh` would fail with EACCES
here. Confirm the exec bit in the real checkout before reading anything into it.

## Automation Path

| Stage | Input | Output | Owner | Terminal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Triage | request + `docs/decisions/` | scoped task with acceptance criteria | agent | criteria stated, or asked |
| Dispatch | scoped task | **missing** — no queue, no task/attempt ID | runner | — |
| Provision | clean checkout | **broken** — `bootstrap.sh` exits non-zero | repository | — |
| Execute | booted service | change under `packages/` | agent | edit complete |
| Prove | booted service | `verify.sh` status + observed responses | repository | zero exit + real-surface observation |
| Submit | proof | **missing** — no artifact schema, no manifest path | repository | — |
| Reconcile | CI or review feedback | **N/A** — no CI on this runner | runner | — |
| Complete | teardown | released PID and port | agent | teardown verified |
| Recover | classified failure | retry ≤2, escalate, or fail | agent | contract added to `AGENTS.md`; unexercised |

First missing transition: **Provision**. Nothing downstream can be proven until
a checkout exists that can bootstrap and boot.

## Files Changed

- `AGENTS.md` — replaced. Model-specific fragments (`For Claude, use XML tags`,
  `For GPT, restate the request`) and the autonomy-blocking `always ask before
  using tools` are gone. Added orientation, a 5-row routing table, authority with
  the local-only boundary, the lifecycle in run order with the two constraints
  the scripts do not enforce, a proof layer table, failure classification, and
  write-back targets. 89 lines.
- `readiness-report.md` — this file.

No product code, script, or credential was touched.

## Remaining Gaps

Highest impact first.

1. **Provision is broken** (repository) — restore `package.json`, `server.js`,
   and `packages/`, or point the scripts at wherever they now live. Everything
   else is blocked behind this.
2. **Teardown kills by name** (repository) — record the PID that `boot.sh`
   started and kill that owned process group; never `pkill -f`. Today it reaps a
   developer's unrelated server. This is a safety blocker for unattended runs,
   and the reason `AGENTS.md` carries a manual pre-check instead.
3. **The gate cannot run cold** (repository) — `verify.sh` curls a service it
   does not boot. Either boot-and-teardown inside verify, or add a read-only
   doctor check that fails with `runner/service_not_running` instead of a bare
   `curl` exit 7.
4. **No cleanup guarantee** (repository) — teardown swallows all errors, so a
   failed release reports success. Cleanup should run on every exit path and
   return non-zero when the primary command succeeded but release did not.
5. **No isolation** (repository) — port `4317` is hardcoded and artifacts have no
   task/attempt path. Two concurrent agents collide.
6. **Write-back targets missing** (repository) — `docs/decisions/` and
   `ops/log.md` are referenced by both guides but do not exist.
7. **Runner cannot execute unattended** (runner) — every script invocation needed
   human approval in this session. A local-only runner that gates each command is
   D by definition; grant the lifecycle commands a standing allowance or run them
   on a runner that can.
8. **`CLAUDE.md` symlink not created** (repository) — one command, still open.

## Path Forward

- To **repository C**: gaps 1 and 6, then run all four scripts cold and record
  exit codes (raises evidence to E1).
- To **repository B**: gaps 2–5, plus one success run and one injected-failure
  run with preserved artifacts and verified final state (E2).
- To **A**: repeated representative trials with outcome graders, two concurrent
  tasks without collision, and exercised crash/stall recovery (E3–E4). Not
  reachable on a local-only runner with no CI.

## Next

Restore `package.json`, `server.js`, and `packages/`, then run
`./scripts/bootstrap.sh` and record its exit code.

# Repair a Private Workspace Agent Contract

## Problem

A private engineering workspace supports Codex, Claude Code, and Grok-based
agents. Its current `AGENTS.md` is generic, model-specific in places, and does
not tell an agent who it is helping, where task context lives, what it may do,
or how to prove work. The repository already has working lifecycle scripts, but
agents regularly rediscover them and sometimes claim completion from a unit test
or screenshot alone.

Audit the workspace for agent readiness and replace `AGENTS.md` with the
smallest useful operating contract. Also produce `readiness-report.md` with the
repository grade, runner grade, evidence level, gaps, and exercised checks.

Do not change product code or invent credentials. Treat the provided runner as
local-only; no CI or live deployment access is available.

## Input Files

=============== FILE: AGENTS.md ===============
# Instructions

You are an expert coding assistant. Think step by step and be concise.
For Claude, use XML tags. For GPT, restate the request before acting.
Read every file before making changes and always ask before using tools.
Write clean code and test your work.

=============== FILE: OWNER.md ===============
# Maya Chen

Maya builds developer tools for small teams. She values simple composable
systems, direct evidence, and finishing the smallest complete useful result.
She often explores too many abstractions before shipping. Private identity and
financial details live under `private/` and should be opened only when a task
requires them.

=============== FILE: docs/workspace.md ===============
# Workspace

Product implementation belongs under `packages/`. Cross-package decisions are
recorded in `docs/decisions/`. Runtime incidents go to `ops/log.md`.

Use `./scripts/bootstrap.sh` for reproducible setup, `./scripts/boot.sh` to
start the local service, `./scripts/verify.sh` for the canonical local gate, and
`./scripts/teardown.sh` for cleanup. CI uses the same verify script.

The API smoke surface is `http://127.0.0.1:4317/health`. Invalid configuration
must exit non-zero with a redacted `config/missing_value` diagnostic.

=============== FILE: scripts/bootstrap.sh ===============
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
test -f package.json

=============== FILE: scripts/boot.sh ===============
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
node server.js

=============== FILE: scripts/verify.sh ===============
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
npm run typecheck
npm test
curl --fail --silent http://127.0.0.1:4317/health

=============== FILE: scripts/teardown.sh ===============
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
pkill -f 'node server.js' 2>/dev/null || true

## Output

Produce:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `readiness-report.md`

assert.value: Human orientation is useful and bounded: AGENTS.md briefly explains Maya's work and translates her simplicity and composition values into a concrete convergence rule such as finishing the smallest complete result before adding abstractions; it treats this as guidance rather than a synthetic persona and points to OWNER.md instead of copying sensitive private facets
Task-shaped routing is present: AGENTS.md tells agents when to read OWNER.md and docs/workspace.md and routes product code, cross-package decisions, and runtime incidents to their declared homes
Shared guidance is model-neutral: AGENTS.md removes per-model XML, restatement, hidden-reasoning, and generic expert-assistant prompt fragments and expresses observable shared behavior instead

Authority is explicit: AGENTS.md allows reversible local work without redundant confirmation, requires a real decision for destructive or external action, and prohibits invented credentials or unnecessary access to private facets
Lifecycle commands are canonical: AGENTS.md names the provided bootstrap, boot, verify, and teardown commands as one coherent repository-owned lifecycle rather than inventing agent-specific wrappers

Proof layers remain separate: AGENTS.md or readiness-report.md distinguishes canonical local guardrails, the health smoke surface, CI, and unavailable live or deploy proof; it does not let a unit test or screenshot imply another layer
Failure quality is part of proof: The contract requires exercising invalid configuration and checking the non-zero redacted config/missing_value diagnostic rather than testing only the happy path

Repository, runner, and evidence are separate: readiness-report.md reports separate repository and runner grades plus an E0-through-E4 evidence level, with each claim bounded by what was actually exercised

Unexercised claims are honest: readiness-report.md does not claim CI, live deployment, repeated autonomy, or a passing command that the fixture does not let it run; missing executable fixture inputs are reported as gaps or static evidence

Guide stays navigational: AGENTS.md is concise but includes the small working model needed to route product code, decisions, incidents, and proof; it uses progressive disclosure and does not copy the entire workspace document, OWNER.md biography, directory tree, or volatile inventory

69	
70	### Legibility
71	
72	- **F:** ownership, commands, or system intent cannot be discovered.
73	- **D:** essential context lives in chat, a wiki, or a person's memory.
74	- **C:** a short repository entrypoint identifies purpose and ownership, then
75	  maps task-shaped routes to current commands and contracts.
76	- **B:** human or product orientation, task acceptance, authority, lifecycle,
77	  verification, ownership, and write-back are versioned, progressively
78	  disclosed, cross-linked, and checked for drift.
79	- **A:** recurring maintenance turns production failures, review feedback, and
80	  architectural drift into updated contracts or mechanical enforcement.
81	
82	### Executability
83	
84	- **F:** the target cannot install or boot.
85	- **D:** setup requires undocumented commands, mutable human profiles, manual env
86	  files, or interactive intervention during normal runs.
87	- **C:** a clean workspace can bootstrap, boot, become ready, and tear down through
88	  documented commands under an explicit runner contract.
89	- **B:** setup is pinned or owned, idempotent, cold-start tested, seedable, and
90	  produces actionable errors for missing repository or runner prerequisites.
91	- **A:** ephemeral and heterogeneous supported runners can self-provision or
92	  self-heal without depending on a named workstation or live user session.
93	
94	### Feedback
95	
96	- **F:** the agent cannot observe whether its work functions.
97	- **D:** only mocked checks, compilation, screenshots without interaction, or
98	  dashboard-only signals exist.
99	- **C:** a smoke or consumer check exercises a real process or shipped artifact.
100	- **B:** canonical local and CI gates cover key real flows, grade final state, and
101	  emit inspectable logs or artifacts with useful failure diagnostics.
102	- **A:** invariants, error paths, production-like or shadow evidence, performance
103	  bounds, and continuous telemetry close the verification loop.
104	
105	### Safety
106	
107	- **F:** required authority is unavailable or the normal path exposes broad secrets.
108	- **D:** agents depend on pasted credentials, shared human sessions, prompt-only
109	  restrictions, open-ended network access, or unclear destructive boundaries.
110	- **C:** required authority and destructive operations are documented and scoped;
111	  secrets are neither printed nor committed, and denied access fails usefully.
112	- **B:** the runner injects a scoped machine or workload identity noninteractively;
113	  sandbox, network, and approval policy enforce the declared task boundary.
114	- **A:** identities are least-privilege per workload or environment, auditable,
115	  revocable and rotatable, isolated across concurrent runs, and continuously checked.
116	
117	### Durability
118	
119	- **F:** failure loses work or leaves the environment unsafe.
120	- **D:** progress depends on a terminal staying open or a human noticing stalls.
121	- **C:** commands have bounded waits, cleanup, explicit artifact paths, and
122	  actionable terminal outcomes.
123	- **B:** task and attempt identity, idempotent setup, durable handoffs, retry caps,
124	  cancellation, and failure classification support unattended completion.
125	- **A:** crash and stall recovery is exercised; sessions, state, and evidence can
126	  be reconstructed without nursing a specific process or container.
127	
128	### Scale
129	
130	- **F:** even one agent collides with existing development or shared resources.
131	- **D:** concurrency requires humans to allocate ports, databases, branches, or accounts.
132	- **C:** one task runs safely in an owned workspace with explicit resource bounds.
133	- **B:** concurrent tasks isolate workspaces, process resources, test state, and
134	  result refs; CI, review, QA, and acceptance feedback can be consumed without babysitting.
135	- **A:** an orchestrator can route triage through dispatch, retries, result
136	  submission and reconciliation, back-pressure, terminal states, and cleanup
137	  with measured cost across implementation and evidence-producing task classes.
138	
139	## Repository and Runner Ownership
140	
141	Grade the owner of a failure, not whichever checkout the audit started in.
142	
143	| Concern | Repository owns | Runner or platform owns |
144	| --- | --- | --- |
145	| Toolchain | version contract and bootstrap command | compatible OS, compute, base tools, caches |
146	| Credentials | required scopes and noninteractive consumption | machine authentication and secret injection |
147	| Workspace | setup, verification, teardown, artifact conventions | isolated filesystem and resource allocation |
148	| Network | declared destinations and useful denied-access behavior | network policy and egress enforcement |
149	| Result submission | artifact/report schemas and branch, PR, CI, review, or acceptance contract | provider credentials, queueing, upload, retry, reconciliation |
150	
151	A pre-provisioned Infisical machine identity, OIDC workload identity, or scoped
152	CI token is positive runner evidence. It is not manual repository setup merely
153	because credentials are required. Human login or profile switching during each
154	run is a runner autonomy gap.
155	
156	Examples:
157	
158	- `repository B / runner D`: bootstrap is correct, but this workstation lacks
159	  the promised machine identity.
160	- `repository B / runner B`: the devbox injects a scoped identity and the repo's
161	  bootstrap consumes it without prompts or secret persistence.
162	- `repository D / runner B`: the runner is ready, but the repo still asks the
163	  agent to hand-create `.env` files or follow a wiki.
164	
165	## Evidence Ceilings and Blockers
166	
167	- Static inspection only (`E0`) cannot justify more than D.
168	- A single exercised command (`E1`) cannot justify more than C.
169	- Real success and failure paths (`E2`) can justify B repository readiness, but
170	  repeated autonomy claims remain provisional.
171	- A requires repeated representative trials (`E3`) and operational recovery or
172	  longitudinal evidence (`E4`) for the claimed task classes.
173	- No real process, shipped-artifact consumer, or final-state grader means
174	  Feedback cannot exceed C.
175	- Unsafe credential exposure, unbounded destructive authority, or an execution
176	  boundary that cannot be established blocks unattended readiness; do not hide
177	  it inside an average.
178	- A missing runner prerequisite in an ad hoc shell is a runner mismatch when the
179	  declared runner contract supplies it. Prove that contract on the real runner
180	  before claiming B or A end to end.
181	
182	## Grading Rules
183	
184	- Grade what agents can actually use, not what files suggest should work.
185	- Prefer cold-start execution over warm developer-machine evidence.
186	- Grade final state and side effects, not an agent's success message.
187	- Accept equivalent mechanisms that satisfy the capability; do not mandate Git
188	  hooks, a particular dead-code tool, worktrees, containers, or port algorithm
189	  without a repository-owned reason.
190	- Keep task classes explicit. A repo may be B for dependency updates, C for UI
191	  changes, and B for scripted QA while remaining D for exploratory device QA.
192	- Record the model, harness, runner, toolchain revision, and evidence date for
193	  empirical claims because capability and scaffolding drift over time.
194
